title: S3-like Object Storage
intro: Think of object storage as a warehouse: `bucket + key` is the address on the waybill, metadata records where the goods are, and data nodes hold the actual bytes. **Finding the address, reading the bytes, and recovering after a disk dies are three different things.**
keyPoints: Metadata and data are separate: the name finds metadata and an object ID, the ID finds a data node, and the node’s index finds the file offset.
Persist the bytes first, then publish metadata: a failure leaves at most a reclaimable orphan; the reverse exposes unreadable broken references.
Synchronous replication keeps acknowledged writes safe but isn’t linearizability: write order, read path, election, and caches need their own rules.
8+4 erasure coding uses 1.5 times the space (50% extra), half of three replicas, at the cost of encoding, decoding, and cross-node reads.
Durability comes from failure-domain placement, checksums, and scrubbing; a checksum only detects damage, so repair needs healthy copies or enough shards.
Sharding by hash(bucket name, object name) favors point lookups; prefix listing fans out and merges. Deletes write a marker first; GC reclaims later.

lessons.title: Storage Types
lessons.summary: Tell storage types apart and estimate object counts

exercises.prompt: An application often modifies a few KB in the middle of a 5 GB file. If the file lives in this chapter’s object storage, what is the only way to update it each time?
options: Send a PUT with an offset and rewrite only those few KB
Rewrite the matching disk blocks on the data node directly
Upload a complete new object over the same key, or create a new version
Mount the bucket as a directory and edit through the file interface
exercises.explanation: This object storage supports only whole-object writes, replacement, and versioning, not in-place partial edits. Workloads that often change bytes in the middle suit block or file storage better; object storage is strongest at write once, read many times.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of data fits object storage best?
options: Huge volumes of user photos and backups, stored and read whole by key
A shared directory mounted by many servers and rewritten often
Database data files that need in-place updates of data pages
A virtual machine’s system disk with low-latency random reads and writes
exercises.explanation: Object storage is built for massive scale, high durability, and low cost, storing and fetching unstructured data whole by key through a RESTful API. VM disks and database files need in-place random rewrites, which suits block storage; a directory mounted by many machines is the classic use of file storage.

exercises.prompt: Match each term with its meaning
pairs: Logical container; name assumed globally unique
The data itself plus its metadata
Keeps several versions of an object in a bucket
The provider’s service commitment to customers
exercises.explanation: A bucket is the logical container for objects, and an object is data plus metadata; versioning lets one key keep several versions in a bucket. An SLA is a contractual commitment, which is not the same thing as design goals such as durability and availability.

exercises.prompt: An object key like `photos/2021/a.jpg` means the bucket contains a real directory named photos.
exercises.explanation: A bucket has no directory hierarchy in the filesystem sense. The `/` is usually just a prefix convention used to simulate paths and list by prefix. Treating it as a POSIX directory leads you to expect whole-directory renames or locks that don’t exist.

exercises.prompt: Six nines of durability and four nines of availability are different goals: data can be intact yet temporarily unreadable.
exercises.explanation: Durability asks whether data is lost over the long run; availability asks whether it can be accessed right now. When a node is down, the data may be intact but unreadable for a while, and a service being online does not mean data was never corrupted. Design and measure the two separately.

exercises.prompt: By count, 20% of objects are under 1 MB, 60% are 1–64 MB, and 20% are over 64 MB, with representative sizes of 0.5, 32, and 200 MB. What is the average object size, roughly?
options: 32 MB
40 MB
exercises.explanation: Weight by share: `0.2×0.5 + 0.6×32 + 0.2×200 = 59.3 MB`. 77.5 MB is the plain average of the three representative values, which ignores that 60% of the objects fall in the 32 MB band.

exercises.prompt: An estimate assumes 100 PB of capacity with 40% used, which gives about 680 million objects. If the 100 PB is entirely actual data instead, about how many objects are there?
options: About 270 million
About 4.2 billion
About 680 million
About 1.7 billion
exercises.explanation: `10^11 MB / 59.3 MB ≈ 1.69×10^9`, about 1.7 billion. The 40% is an assumption about used capacity; if the 100 PB is already actual data, you should not multiply by 0.4 again. The 270 million figure applies 40% a second time to 680 million.

exercises.prompt: Complete the metadata size estimate
exercises.text: At 40% used capacity there are about [[680 million]] objects; at 1 KB of metadata each, the total metadata is about [[0.68 TB]].
exercises.explanation: `680 million × 1 KB ≈ 680 billion bytes ≈ 0.68 TB`. Next to 100 PB of data, the metadata is tiny, but it has a huge number of entries and is queried often, so the object table still needs sharding and the bucket table needs more read throughput.

exercises.prompt: A 7200 rpm SATA disk can do roughly 100–150 random seeks per second. What is this number best used to estimate?
options: A disk’s annual failure rate
The throughput ceiling for large sequential reads and writes
The IOPS ceiling for small-object random reads and writes
The total disk capacity the whole cluster needs
exercises.explanation: Object storage can be limited by capacity or by IOPS. The number of random seeks decides how many small random I/Os a disk completes per second, and with huge numbers of small objects it often becomes the bottleneck before capacity does. Sequential I/O doesn’t seek repeatedly, so you can’t derive throughput from this number.

exercises.prompt: Which of these features does this problem’s object storage need to support?
options: Mount a bucket as a POSIX file system
Modify part of an object’s bytes in place
List the objects in a bucket
Create a bucket
Object versioning
exercises.explanation: The features from requirements clarification are: create buckets, upload/download, versioning, and listing the objects in a bucket. Partial in-place modification is out of scope, since an object can only be replaced whole; POSIX mounting is a file storage capability.

lessons.title: Read/Write Path
lessons.summary: How a PUT/GET flows and how bytes get replicated

exercises.prompt: Object storage keeps metadata and object content in two separate stores. What is the main benefit?
options: Reading an object touches only one system, saving a network round trip
Metadata and bytes fit in one transaction, so they are consistent by nature
Objects can therefore be modified partially in place
The two have different access patterns, so each scales and is tuned independently
exercises.explanation: Metadata is small and queried often; content is large and mostly read or written whole. Separating them lets each side scale against its own bottleneck. The cost: a read needs an extra hop to metadata, and a write spans two systems with no shared transaction, hence orphan objects.

exercises.prompt: Match each high-level component with its responsibility
pairs: Spreads API requests across service replicas
Stores and fetches real bytes by object UUID
Records buckets, object names, and object IDs
exercises.explanation: The API service holds no state: it calls IAM for auth first, then talks to the metadata store and the data store. The data store knows only UUIDs, not bucket or object names; the mapping from name to ID lives in the metadata store.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of uploading the object `script.txt` in order (the bucket already exists)
items: The client sends a PUT request to the API service
IAM verifies the identity and write permission
The data store persists the body and returns a UUID
The metadata store records object ID, bucket ID, and name
Success is returned to the client
exercises.explanation: Authenticate first, then write the bytes. Once the bytes are durable and a UUID comes back, publish the metadata, and only then reply with success. Writing bytes before publishing metadata means a failure leaves at most a reclaimable orphan, never an object users can see but cannot read.

exercises.prompt: When handling `GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt`, what key piece of information does the API service get back from the metadata store?
options: The object’s UUID, used to fetch the bytes from the data store
The full byte content of the object
The object’s file name and offset on the data node
Whether the caller has read permission
exercises.explanation: The path is bucket/key, then the metadata store returns the object UUID, then the data store fetches the bytes by UUID. File names and offsets belong to the data node’s internal local index, which global metadata doesn’t track; read permission is checked by IAM.

exercises.prompt: In an upload, making the metadata visible first and persisting the bytes afterward is more dangerous than writing the bytes first and committing the metadata afterward.
exercises.explanation: If the bytes are written but the metadata commit fails, you are left with an unreferenced orphan that can be reclaimed later. If the metadata is published before the bytes are durable, users see a broken reference that can’t be read. Better an extra box with no waybill than a waybill with no box.

exercises.prompt: The three replicas of object O9 are written. While committing the metadata `photo.jpg → O9`, the connection drops and the client gets a timeout. What is the safest next step?
options: Assume the commit succeeded and return success to the client
Generate a new object ID and write the data again
Check the commit status first, then retry idempotently if it did not commit
Delete O9 immediately and make the client upload from scratch
exercises.explanation: A timeout doesn’t mean the commit failed: it may have succeeded with only the response lost. Check with a stable upload/request ID, then retry idempotently. Deleting O9 might destroy a legitimate object; a new ID leaves an extra copy; reporting success outright may be false and the object unreadable.

exercises.prompt: The placement service is replicated with Raft, with 5 or 7 replicas recommended. If you deploy 5 replicas, how many node failures can it tolerate at most while a majority can still communicate?
options: 3 nodes
2 nodes
1 node
4 nodes
exercises.explanation: Consensus requires a surviving majority: with 5 nodes at least 3 must be healthy, so at most 2 can fail; with 7 nodes at least 4 must be healthy, so at most 3 can fail. The placement service holds the virtual cluster map and is a critical component, so it is replicated with consensus.

exercises.prompt: Put the flow of writing object bytes into the data store in order
items: The API service passes the object to the routing service
The routing service sends it to the group’s primary
The primary copies it to two replicas and waits
The data store returns the object UUID to the API service
exercises.explanation: The routing service first picks the replica group, then hands the data to the primary. The primary replies only after both replicas have copied the data, so getting a UUID back means several copies are on disk. Waiting for replication adds write latency: you trade latency for durability.

exercises.prompt: For “a read after a successful write always sees the new value” to hold, what must be specified besides writing synchronously to three replicas?
options: Switch to 8+4 erasure coding
A single order and commit point for concurrent writes to the same key
A read path that returns only a committed, sufficiently recent version
Fencing off the old primary with a term during failover
Raise the replica count from 3 to 5
exercises.explanation: The replica count only answers how many copies of the data exist. Which version of history a read sees depends on write ordering, the read path, and election rules, and a cache must not bypass them. Adding replicas or switching to erasure coding changes only durability and space; it can’t fix reading a stale version.

exercises.prompt: When the placement service sees a data node’s heartbeat time out, that proves the data on the node is permanently lost.
exercises.explanation: A heartbeat timeout means only a suspected failure: it may be network flapping, a stalled process, or a partition, and the data on disk may be intact. Handle it using the timeout, the node’s identity or term, and a rejoin procedure, so you don’t re-create replicas while the old primary keeps accepting writes.

lessons.title: Node Durability
lessons.summary: Storing small objects; replication vs erasure coding

exercises.prompt: Why don’t data nodes store one file per object, and instead append small objects into files of several GB?
options: Large files naturally support listing by key prefix
It reduces wasted block space and inode overhead
Deleting an object frees its disk space immediately
Large files allow partial in-place modification of objects
exercises.explanation: Filesystems allocate in blocks, so a 1 KB object still takes a typical 4 KB block, and hundreds of millions of small files also mean hundreds of millions of inodes. Appending to large files cuts both space and management overhead, at the cost that deletion doesn’t free space at once and compaction is needed to reclaim it.

exercises.prompt: Many CPU cores append objects to the same data file at once, so writes must be serialized and throughput stalls. What improvement does this chapter give?
options: Raise the file rollover threshold above a few GB
Go back to one file per object
Take a global lock before every append
Let different cores append to different files
exercises.explanation: The bottleneck is that appends to one file must be serial. Giving each core its own file removes the lock contention. Raising the rollover threshold doesn’t change the contention; a global lock is the serialization itself; one file per object returns to the small-file problem.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two-level mapping used to locate an object
exercises.text: Global metadata maps the bucket name and object name to the [[object ID]]; the data node’s local index then maps it to the [[file and offset]], from which the bytes are read.
exercises.explanation: The name finds metadata and an object ID, the ID locates a data node, and the node then looks up the file offset. The local index records `object_id`, `filename`, `file_offset`, and `object_size`; it covers only this node’s objects and is not global metadata.

exercises.prompt: Each data node only looks up the objects it stores, so it can embed SQLite for its local index instead of having every node share one remote mapping database.
exercises.explanation: A shared remote database would have to serve the whole cluster’s queries, with an extra network round trip on every read. A local index covers only this node’s objects, so an embedded database is enough. Whether to pick SQLite or RocksDB should be settled by measuring concurrency, recovery, and persistence cost.

exercises.prompt: A data node appends an object to `/data/c`, then inserts a record into the mapping table. These two steps naturally form an atomic transaction, so nothing is inconsistent after a crash.
exercises.explanation: A file append and a database insert live in two different systems and are not a transaction by themselves: the file may be written without the index entry, or the index may commit before the file reaches disk. Recovery after a restart relies on logs, flush ordering, object boundaries, and checksums.

exercises.prompt: The chapter takes an HDD annual failure rate of 0.81% and concludes that three replicas reach about six nines, estimating the loss probability as `0.0081³`. Which assumption does this calculation depend on most?
options: Every disk is read and written sequentially
Metadata and data are stored separately
Data is written to the primary first and then replicated
The failures of the three replicas are independent
exercises.explanation: Multiplying the three probabilities requires failures to be uncorrelated. If all three replicas sit in one rack, one power outage loses them all, which is why you spread them across failure domains such as racks and data centers. Repair windows, silent corruption, and operator error also push real risk above the formula.

exercises.prompt: An 800 MB object is stored with 8+4 erasure coding. How much space does it take in total? (Ignore metadata and alignment padding.)
exercises.explanation: Cut into 8 shards of 100 MB each, then generate 4 parity shards of the same size: 12 shards, 1,200 MB in total, which is 1.5 times the original and 50% extra. 2,400 MB is what three replicas take, so 8+4 uses only half the space of three replicas.

exercises.prompt: Compared with three replicas, what does 8+4 erasure coding cost you?
options: Extra computation for encoding, decoding, and checksums
A larger total storage footprint
Higher implementation complexity
Reads and repairs must touch shards on multiple nodes
Fewer simultaneous node failures tolerated than three replicas
exercises.explanation: Erasure coding trades computation and cross-node access for space: reads fetch shards from several nodes and may decode; repairs pull many shards. It uses 1.5 times the space, versus 3 times for three replicas. 8+4 tolerates any 4 missing shards while three replicas can lose only 2 copies, so its fault tolerance is not worse.

exercises.prompt: Service A has little data but needs very low read latency; service B is a petabyte-scale archive that is rarely read. According to this chapter, which redundancy scheme does each lean toward?
options: Both use three replicas
A uses replicas, B uses erasure coding
A uses erasure coding, B uses replicas
Both use erasure coding
exercises.explanation: A replica can serve a whole object from one node, so latency is low but it takes 3 times the space. Erasure coding saves space, but reads and repairs span nodes and need computation. So latency-sensitive workloads lean toward replication, and cost-sensitive large-scale storage leans toward erasure coding.

exercises.prompt: A checksum can detect silent corruption, but repairing it still requires a healthy replica or enough valid shards.
exercises.explanation: Recomputing and comparing the checksum on read only tells you the data is bad. Repair relies on another intact replica, or on rebuilding from at least 8 valid shards in 8+4. Periodic scrubbing finds problems before a second failure; data that fails verification is quarantined first, never deleted if it is the only copy left.

lessons.title: Metadata & GC
lessons.summary: Sharding, listing, versions, multipart upload, and GC

exercises.prompt: If the object table is sharded by `bucket_id`, what problem is most likely?
options: Objects in one bucket cannot be listed by prefix
The bucket table grows too large for a single database
Looking up one object by bucket name and object name queries every shard
One huge bucket with billions of objects overwhelms its shard
exercises.explanation: Sharding by bucket puts all objects of a bucket in one shard, so a huge bucket becomes a hotspot. Its upside is exactly that single-bucket point lookups and listings hit just one shard. Buckets are usually limited in number, so the bucket table fits in one database; it is the object table that needs sharding.

exercises.prompt: The object table is finally sharded by `hash(bucket_name, object_name)`. Which operation becomes slower as a result?
options: Deleting one object by bucket name and object name
Listing the objects in a bucket whose key prefix is `abc/`
Finding one object by bucket name and object name
Uploading a new object and writing its metadata
exercises.explanation: Point lookups, inserts, and deletes all carry the bucket and object name, so the hash sends them straight to one shard. But objects in the same bucket with the same prefix are scattered over all shards, so listing must query each shard and merge in memory. This is the trade-off between balanced point lookups and range locality.

exercises.prompt: After hash sharding, which approaches deal with listing a bucket’s objects becoming slow or hard to paginate?
options: Go back to sharding by bucket_id and ignore hotspots
Query every shard and merge in memory, accepting slower listing
Use sorted cursors and per-shard positions instead of large offsets
Build a separate denormalized listing table partitioned by bucket
Query only one shard and return the full result
exercises.explanation: Two paths work: accept fan-out and merge, or build a separate listing table partitioned by bucket. In pagination each shard returns a different number of rows, so a sorted cursor that remembers each shard’s position beats a large offset. Querying one shard misses data; bucket sharding brings back the big-bucket hotspot.

exercises.prompt: A bucket has versioning on, and a user deletes the object `report.pdf`. What does the system do by default?
options: Mark all versions of the object read-only
Roll the current version back to the previous version
Physically delete the bytes of all versions at once
Insert a delete marker as the newest version
exercises.explanation: Deleting just inserts a special delete marker as the newest version, so a default GET sees it and returns 404. The old version bytes remain and may still be read by version number; space is freed only by lifecycle cleanup and GC. It also does not “restore” the previous version as the current one.

exercises.prompt: Two clients upload new versions of the same key at almost the same moment. The system can use each client’s local clock to decide which version is newer.
exercises.explanation: Client clocks can drift or even be tampered with, so they can’t decide version order. `object_version` uses a TIMEUUID so versions sort by time, but the order of concurrent versions of one key should be decided by server-side rules, so that every reader sees the same “latest version.”

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a multipart upload of a large file in order
items: The client sends an initiation request
The server returns a unique upload_id
The client uploads each part with the upload_id
The server returns an ETag for each successful part
The client commits the upload_id, part numbers, and ETags
The server assembles the object and returns success
exercises.explanation: Parts travel independently, and a failure retransmits only that part. The commit must carry every part number and ETag, so each part must have returned its ETag first. The full object becomes visible only after the commit, and uncommitted temporary parts are cleaned up by garbage collection.

exercises.prompt: A client uploads a file in two parts, then compares `md5(local file)` with the returned ETag and finds they differ. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The ETag of a multipart upload is not an MD5 of the whole file in the first place
The local file was modified during the upload
The server missed the last part when computing the MD5
One part was corrupted in transit; delete the object and re-upload
exercises.explanation: An ETag is an identifier defined by the service. For multipart uploads and some encryption modes it is not the MD5 of the full bytes (it often has a part-count suffix), so a mismatch doesn’t show corruption. To verify integrity, use a declared checksum algorithm and check whether it covers the whole object or combines parts.

exercises.prompt: If one part fails during a multipart upload, you only need to resend that part with the same upload_id instead of uploading the whole file again.
exercises.explanation: The point of multipart upload is that parts transfer and retry independently, and parts that already succeeded are kept. Once all parts are in, you commit the part list, and the object becomes visible only after the server has assembled it, so readers never see half a file.

exercises.prompt: What space can the garbage collector reclaim?
options: Space held by objects whose deletion was deferred
Orphaned data left by failed uploads and confirmed to have no references
A new upload whose bytes were just written but whose metadata isn’t published yet
An old file whose mapping was switched but is still used by in-flight reads
Corrupted replicas confirmed to be replaceable
exercises.explanation: GC reclaims deferred deletions, orphans from failed uploads, and corrupted replicas that can be replaced. A new upload by design writes bytes before publishing metadata, so having no reference at this instant isn’t proof of garbage, and an old file must wait for in-flight reads. Reclamation lags behind visibility.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of one compaction (merging and cleaning up files) in order
items: Pick old files that reach the compaction threshold
Copy still-valid objects from the old files to a new file
Point object_mapping to the new location in a transaction
Free the old files after in-flight reads finish
exercises.explanation: First copy the valid objects, and switch the mapping only after the new file is durable, so readers can always find the data. Switch the mapping in one transaction so nothing is half old, half new. An old file may still be being read, so it can’t be deleted at the instant of the switch.
